The three tables above are filled in for three different data types, and only the first describes this analysis. The second and third are kept in the unit because every student in the group will write one of those papers eventually, and because a filled checklist is easier to adapt than an empty one.

comp <- rbind(
  data.frame(checklist = sprintf("OECD (%d)", nrow(oecd)), status = oecd$status),
  data.frame(checklist = sprintf("TRIPOD+AI (%d)", nrow(tripod)), status = tripod$status))
comp <- as.data.frame(table(comp$checklist, comp$status)); names(comp) <- c("checklist", "status", "n")
comp$status <- factor(comp$status, levels = c("met", "partly", "n/a"))
print(ggplot(comp[comp$n > 0, ], aes(n, checklist, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.45) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), colour = "white", size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(met = "#009E73", partly = "#E69F00", `n/a` = "#999999")) +
  labs(x = "checklist items", y = NULL, fill = NULL, title = "Reporting compliance of this analysis"))

cat("OECD:", paste(sprintf("%s=%d", names(table(oecd$status)), as.integer(table(oecd$status))), collapse = " "), "\n")
## OECD: met=3 partly=2
cat("TRIPOD+AI:", paste(sprintf("%s=%d", names(table(tripod$status)), as.integer(table(tripod$status))), collapse = " "), "\n")
## TRIPOD+AI: met=9 n/a=1 partly=1
cat("MIAME/MINSEQE and LiveCoMS are not scored here: this analysis contains neither omics nor simulation,\n")
## MIAME/MINSEQE and LiveCoMS are not scored here: this analysis contains neither omics nor simulation,
cat("and a checklist reported as satisfied for data you do not have is worse than no checklist.\n")
## and a checklist reported as satisfied for data you do not have is worse than no checklist.

Figure 9. Items of the two applicable checklists, classified as fully met, partly met or not applicable. The orange segments are the honest part of the figure: an applicability domain defined in another unit rather than here, an absent sample-size justification and an uncommitted mechanistic interpretation are the items this analysis would be asked about in review. The two checklists that do not apply to this data type are left unscored.

13. Availability, licences and preprints

Two short statements at the end of a paper do more for its reuse than any amount of Discussion. A data-availability statement says where the data are, under what identifier, and what a reader must do to get them; “available from the authors on reasonable request” is, empirically, a statement that the data are not available[20][21]. The target is the FAIR standard — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable[18] — and the incentive is not only ethical: papers with openly deposited data are cited measurably more often[19]. A code-availability statement names a repository, a release tag or commit and, ideally, an archival DOI from a service such as Zenodo, because a GitHub repository can be deleted and a DOI cannot.

Licences are where the laboratory’s own obligations appear. ChEMBL data are distributed under CC BY-SA 3.0, a share-alike licence: a curated table derived from ChEMBL must be redistributed under the same terms, and quietly putting it under CC BY or under no licence at all is a licence violation, not an oversight. Code in the group is released under the MIT licence unless a dependency forces otherwise, and figures under CC BY 4.0.

avail <- paste(c(
 "Data availability. The curated ROCK1 activity table analysed in this study was derived from ChEMBL release",
 sprintf("37 (target CHEMBL3231) and is deposited with the analysis code (file rock1_chembl_curated.csv, %d rows,", nrow(df)),
 sprintf("SHA-256 %s...). ChEMBL is distributed under CC BY-SA 3.0; the derived table is redistributed under", substr(raw_sha, 1, 24)),
 "the same licence. Supplementary Table S1 contains the per-compound predictions of the hold-out set",
 sprintf("(%d rows, SHA-256 %s...) and its data dictionary.", nrow(supp), substr(sha_s1, 1, 16)),
 "",
 "Code availability. All analyses were performed with the R Markdown document deposited at",
 "https://github.com/<organisation>/<repository> (release v1.0.0, archived at Zenodo under",
 "doi:10.5281/zenodo.<id>), licensed under the MIT licence. The document reproduces every figure and every",
 "number reported here from the deposited data in under five minutes on a laptop.",
 "",
 "Author contributions, competing interests and funding are reported in the sections required by the journal."),
 collapse = "\n")
cat(avail, "\n\n")
## Data availability. The curated ROCK1 activity table analysed in this study was derived from ChEMBL release
## 37 (target CHEMBL3231) and is deposited with the analysis code (file rock1_chembl_curated.csv, 4280 rows,
## SHA-256 765ab0cf633b4dd26a9be200...). ChEMBL is distributed under CC BY-SA 3.0; the derived table is redistributed under
## the same licence. Supplementary Table S1 contains the per-compound predictions of the hold-out set
## (553 rows, SHA-256 3219b4ea22697cf4...) and its data dictionary.
## 
## Code availability. All analyses were performed with the R Markdown document deposited at
## https://github.com/<organisation>/<repository> (release v1.0.0, archived at Zenodo under
## doi:10.5281/zenodo.<id>), licensed under the MIT licence. The document reproduces every figure and every
## number reported here from the deposited data in under five minutes on a laptop.
## 
## Author contributions, competing interests and funding are reported in the sections required by the journal.
lic <- data.frame(
  artefact = c("Source data (ChEMBL)", "Curated table and supplement", "Analysis code",
               "Figures and text of the paper", "Trained model artefacts"),
  licence = c("CC BY-SA 3.0", "CC BY-SA 3.0", "MIT", "CC BY 4.0", "CC BY-SA 3.0"),
  obligation = c("share-alike: derived tables must carry the same licence", "inherited from the source",
                 "permissive; compatible with reuse in commercial settings",
                 "attribution only; required by most open-access journals",
                 "a model trained on share-alike data inherits the obligation"))
kable(lic, col.names = c("artefact", "licence", "what it obliges"))
artefact licence what it obliges
Source data (ChEMBL) CC BY-SA 3.0 share-alike: derived tables must carry the same licence
Curated table and supplement CC BY-SA 3.0 inherited from the source
Analysis code MIT permissive; compatible with reuse in commercial settings
Figures and text of the paper CC BY 4.0 attribution only; required by most open-access journals
Trained model artefacts CC BY-SA 3.0 a model trained on share-alike data inherits the obligation

The statement above contains four things a reuser needs and most statements omit: the release of the source database, the file name, its checksum and its licence. A preprint is the third element. Posting to ChemRxiv, bioRxiv or arXiv at submission establishes priority and makes the work citable while it is in review; almost every journal the laboratory targets permits it, and the exceptions are listed in the journal’s policy page, to be checked before posting rather than after.

14. The abstract, and the ladder of claims

The abstract is read a hundred times for every time the paper is read, so it is written last and rewritten most. A structured four-move abstract fits any computational paper: what problem and why it matters (two sentences), what was done (two sentences, with the data size), what was found (two or three sentences, with the key numbers and their uncertainty), and what it means and for whom (one sentence, bounded by the applicability domain). The hardest discipline is the last move, because it is where over-claiming lives.

The ladder of claims is a device the group uses in internal review. For any result, write the claim at four strengths and choose the highest one the evidence supports: (1) “we observed”, (2) “the model ranks”, (3) “the model predicts”, (4) “the model enables”. Evidence of a scaffold-split RMSE somewhat above the experimental noise floor supports rung two comfortably, rung three with the domain stated, and rung four not at all without prospective validation.

abstract <- paste(c(
 "Rho-associated kinase 1 (ROCK1) is a therapeutic target in glaucoma, fibrosis and cardiovascular disease,",
 "and public bioactivity data for it are large enough to support ligand-based models but heterogeneous enough",
 sprintf("to mislead them. We curated %d compounds with measured ROCK1 affinity from ChEMBL 37 (%d with exact", nrow(df), nrow(ex)),
 sprintf("values) and estimated the experimental error floor of the data at %.2f log units from replicate", sigma_exp),
 sprintf("measurements. A random forest on Morgan fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors reached an RMSE of %.2f", rmse_cv),
 sprintf("log units under random five-fold cross-validation, but %.2f [%.2f, %.2f] on a Bemis-Murcko scaffold hold-out",
         rmse_sc, ci_rmse[2], ci_rmse[3]),
 sprintf("of %d compounds sharing no scaffold with the training set, with R2 %.2f. Selecting the 10 top-ranked", length(TE), r2_sc),
 sprintf("hold-out compounds recovered a potent fraction of %.2f against a base rate of %.2f. The model therefore", hits[1], base_rate),
 "ranks unseen chemotypes usefully while predicting their absolute potency to little better than the measurement",
 "error, and we report it with its applicability domain, its uncertainty and the code that produced it."),
 collapse = "\n")
cat(abstract)
## Rho-associated kinase 1 (ROCK1) is a therapeutic target in glaucoma, fibrosis and cardiovascular disease,
## and public bioactivity data for it are large enough to support ligand-based models but heterogeneous enough
## to mislead them. We curated 4280 compounds with measured ROCK1 affinity from ChEMBL 37 (2764 with exact
## values) and estimated the experimental error floor of the data at 0.51 log units from replicate
## measurements. A random forest on Morgan fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors reached an RMSE of 0.73
## log units under random five-fold cross-validation, but 0.86 [0.80, 0.91] on a Bemis-Murcko scaffold hold-out
## of 553 compounds sharing no scaffold with the training set, with R2 0.31. Selecting the 10 top-ranked
## hold-out compounds recovered a potent fraction of 0.80 against a base rate of 0.19. The model therefore
## ranks unseen chemotypes usefully while predicting their absolute potency to little better than the measurement
## error, and we report it with its applicability domain, its uncertainty and the code that produced it.
n_words <- lengths(gregexpr("\\S+", abstract))
cat(sprintf("\n\n[%d words | sample sizes present: %s | uncertainty reported: %s | bounded claims: %d]\n",
            n_words, grepl("[0-9]{3,4}", abstract), grepl("\\[", abstract),
            sum(vapply(c("therefore", "while", "little better"),
                       function(w) lengths(gregexpr(w, abstract, fixed = TRUE)), numeric(1)))))
## 
## 
## [159 words | sample sizes present: TRUE | uncertainty reported: TRUE | bounded claims: 3]
cat("rung of the claim ladder used: 2-3 ('ranks usefully', 'predicts to little better than the error')\n")
## rung of the claim ladder used: 2-3 ('ranks usefully', 'predicts to little better than the error')

That abstract is deliberately unexciting, and it is the version that survives review. It contains the two numbers a referee will look for (the optimistic one and the honest one), it reports an interval, and its final sentence states both what the model does and what it does not do. An abstract claiming that the model “accurately predicts ROCK1 inhibition” would use the same experiments and would be false at rung four.

15. Large language models: disclosure, and the reference check you must run

Language models are now part of how most of this material is written and coded, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. The publishers the group submits to have converged on three rules[23][24]: a language model cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility; its use must be disclosed, usually in the Methods or an Acknowledgements-adjacent statement; and the authors remain fully responsible for every sentence, every number and every citation in the manuscript. Surveys of researchers show the practice is widespread and the disclosure is not[22].

The laboratory’s position is practical. A language model is an acceptable tool for improving the English of a paragraph you wrote, for drafting boilerplate, for explaining an error message and for suggesting code that you then test. It is not an acceptable tool for generating results, for writing a Discussion you have not thought through, or — above all — for producing citations. The characteristic failure mode is a plausible reference: correct-looking authors, a real journal, a DOI that is either nonexistent or belongs to a different paper, at rates high enough that an automated check is now part of the group’s submission routine[25].

That check is twenty lines of R. For every DOI in the bibliography, ask Crossref what the title of that DOI is, and compare it with the title in your reference list. The next chunk runs it on a short bibliography into which two bad entries have been planted: one DOI that does not exist, and one real DOI attached to the wrong title. The Python edition used difflib; R has no equivalent in base, so the comparison uses a normalised Levenshtein distance from utils::adist(), which gives a slightly different similarity for the same pair of strings but the same verdicts at the same threshold.

BIB <- list(
  c("10.1021/ci400197w", "Modeling, informatics, and the quest for reproducibility"),
  c("10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619", "Ten simple rules for structuring papers"),
  c("10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7", "Reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences"),
  c("10.1136/bmj-2023-078378", paste("TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction",
                                     "models that use regression or machine learning methods")),
  c("10.1021/jm300131x", "A deep learning framework for ROCK1 inhibitor design"),      ## planted: wrong title
  c("10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9", "Graph neural networks predict kinase selectivity")) ## planted: no such DOI
FROZEN <- list("10.1021/ci400197w" = "Modeling, Informatics, and the Quest for Reproducibility",
               "10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619" = "Ten simple rules for structuring papers",
               "10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7" = "Reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences",
               "10.1136/bmj-2023-078378" = paste("TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical",
                                                 "prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods"),
               "10.1021/jm300131x" = "The Experimental Uncertainty of Heterogeneous Public Ki Data",
               "10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9" = NA_character_)
normalise <- function(t) {
  t <- gsub("<[^>]+>", " ", tolower(ifelse(is.na(t), "", t)))
  gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(gsub("[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", t)))
}
crossref_title <- function(doi) {
  resp <- request("https://api.crossref.org/works/") |> req_url_path_append(doi) |>
    req_user_agent("LBQC course material (reference integrity check)") |>
    req_timeout(12) |> req_perform()
  resp_body_json(resp)$message$title[[1]]
}
live <- tryCatch({ crossref_title(BIB[[1]][1]); TRUE }, error = function(e) FALSE)
rows <- lapply(BIB, function(bb) {
  found <- if (live) tryCatch(crossref_title(bb[1]), error = function(e) NA_character_) else FROZEN[[bb[1]]]
  a <- normalise(bb[2]); b <- normalise(found)
  sim <- if (is.na(found)) 0 else 1 - as.numeric(adist(a, b)) / max(nchar(a), nchar(b))
  data.frame(doi = bb[1], similarity = round(sim, 2),
             verdict = if (is.na(found)) "DOI NOT FOUND" else if (sim >= 0.75) "ok" else "TITLE MISMATCH",
             registered_title = substr(ifelse(is.na(found), "-", found), 1, 46))
})
check <- do.call(rbind, rows)
cat(sprintf("path taken: %s\n", if (live) "live Crossref queries" else "frozen fallback list"))
## path taken: live Crossref queries
kable(check)
doi similarity verdict registered_title
10.1021/ci400197w 1.0 ok Modeling, Informatics, and the Quest for Repro
10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619 1.0 ok Ten simple rules for structuring papers
10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7 1.0 ok Reproducibility standards for machine learning
10.1136/bmj-2023-078378 1.0 ok TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for repo
10.1021/jm300131x 0.2 TITLE MISMATCH The Experimental Uncertainty of Heterogeneous
10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9 0.0 DOI NOT FOUND - 
cat(sprintf("flagged %d of %d entries\n", sum(check$verdict != "ok"), nrow(check)))
## flagged 2 of 6 entries
check$lab <- sprintf("%s  [%s]", check$doi, check$verdict)
check$lab <- factor(check$lab, levels = rev(check$lab))
print(ggplot(check, aes(similarity, lab, fill = verdict == "ok")) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.75, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.76, y = 6.4, hjust = 0, size = 2.4, label = "acceptance threshold 0.75") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#009E73", `FALSE` = "#D55E00")) +
  xlim(0, 1.25) + labs(x = "title similarity to the registered record", y = NULL,
                       title = "Reference-integrity check of a six-entry bibliography") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6)))

cat("entries below the threshold:", paste(check$doi[check$verdict != "ok"], collapse = ", "), "\n")
## entries below the threshold: 10.1021/jm300131x, 10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9

Figure 10. Title similarity between each bibliography entry and the record registered for its DOI. Four entries match closely; the fifth is a real DOI (a 2012 paper on the experimental uncertainty of public affinity data) carrying a fabricated title, and the sixth is a DOI that was never registered. Both planted errors are caught, and neither would have been caught by reading the reference list.

The threshold of 0.75 is a choice, not a law: subtitles, non-ASCII characters and markup in the registered record depress the similarity of good entries, which is why the check flags rather than deletes — and why the character-level measure used here is more conservative than the token-level one of the Python edition for titles that differ only in capitalisation or punctuation. Run it before every submission; it catches errors copied from a slide deck or a colleague’s manuscript as readily as those from a language model.

A worked disclosure statement, in the form the laboratory uses:

Statement on the use of generative tools

During the preparation of this work the authors used a large language model to improve the readability and the English style of several paragraphs of the Introduction and Discussion, and to draft documentation comments in the analysis code. All text was subsequently reviewed and edited by the authors, every reference was verified against its registered Crossref record, and all code was tested against the unit tests in the deposited repository. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

16. Summary

The last mile is computation, not decoration. Figures, tables, the Methods paragraph, the availability statements, the checklists and even the abstract were generated here from the analysis that produced the results, and the ones that are generated stay correct when the results change.

Figures are physical objects. Draw at the final width in centimetres with ggsave(units = "cm"), set the font size once in a theme function, export vector with cairo_pdf so the fonts are embedded — the default pdf() device does not embed them — and check the figure under colour-vision deficiency and in greyscale before it is submitted[1][6][8]. The remake in Section 5 changed nothing about the data and everything about what a reader can take from it.

The misleading figure is the dangerous one. A truncated axis turned a difference of a fraction of a log unit — smaller than the experimental noise, with a confidence interval containing zero — into a visual factor of several, and a bar of means hid two almost completely overlapping distributions[5]. Bars start at zero; means travel with their distributions; differences are plotted against the noise floor.

Digits are claims. Round the uncertainty first, then the value; report an error in the units of the target, a rank metric, the sample size and the split; and never let a single flattering metric stand for the model’s performance[2].

Checklists are cheap insurance. OECD and QMRF for QSAR[12][13], TRIPOD+AI for clinical prediction[10], MIAME and MINSEQE for omics[11], LiveCoMS for simulation[15][16]: fill in the applicable one, mark partly-met items honestly, leave the rest unscored.

Disclose the tools and verify the references. A language model is a writing and coding assistant whose use is disclosed and whose output is checked; the reference-integrity check of Section 15 is twenty lines of httr2 and catches the one error that most damages a manuscript’s credibility[25].

What follows this unit is the machinery that makes the claims checkable by someone else: Unit 24 turns the analysis code into a tested R package, Unit 25 into a workflow that runs on a cluster, and Unit 26 into a tool a collaborator can use — each with its own form of documentation, and each pointing back at the figures and numbers assembled here.

Bridge

The evidence communicated here was built earlier in this course and in its sister courses. The exploratory figure remade in Section 5 comes from Unit 5; the experimental error floor and the data card from Unit 6; the scaffold split and the honest metric from Unit 12; the model from Unit 14; the applicability domain and the OECD discussion from Unit 17; the enrichment panel from the virtual-screening unit, U19 of the Python edition; the simulation reporting items from U20 and the omics ones from U21. In the cheminformatics course, Data curation and Validation cover the chemistry-specific reporting that referees at cheminformatics journals expect, and Classical QSAR the QMRF tradition. In the bioinformatics course, Molecular dynamics supplies the simulation protocol details that LiveCoMS asks you to report, and in the R edition of the AI course Model evaluation covers the metric definitions quoted in the tables above. The Python edition of this unit is here.

17. Self-assessment

  1. A journal asks for figures at 300 dpi, maximum width 8.5 cm. You drew your figure with the device defaults. What exactly goes wrong, and what is the fix?

R’s default device is 7 inches = 17.8 cm wide, so the typesetter scales it by about 0.48. Every font, line width and marker shrinks by the same factor: a 9-point label arrives at about 4.3 points, below the publisher’s minimum, and hairlines disappear. Enlarging the fonts afterwards changes the layout. The fix is ggsave(file, plot, width = 8.5, height = h, units = “cm”), choosing the base font size at that size with theme_lbqc(), and exporting vector (PDF) so the dpi requirement applies only to raster panels.

  1. Why is a PDF usually smaller than a 300 dpi PNG of the same scatter plot, and when is the reverse true?

A PDF stores one drawing instruction per mark, a PNG stores every pixel of the canvas. With a few thousand marks the instructions win, as measured in Section 2. The reverse is true once the number of marks approaches the number of pixels — tens of thousands of points, a dense heat map, a rendered molecular surface — which is when rasterising the heavy data layer while keeping the axes and text vector is the right compromise.

  1. In R, which device do you use to export a figure with embedded fonts, and how do you check?

cairo_pdf (or ggsave(…, device = cairo_pdf)); the default pdf() device references the base-14 fonts by name instead of embedding them. The check is three lines: read the file as raw bytes and search for the string /FontFile, as the first chunk of Section 2 does — it is TRUE for the cairo file and FALSE for the default one.

  1. Your supervisor says the two scaffold families in Figure 5 “clearly differ in potency”. What do you answer, with numbers?

The difference of means is a fraction of a log unit, its bootstrap confidence interval includes zero, Cohen’s d is small, and the experimental standard deviation of a single measurement is several times the difference itself. The honest statement is that the two families are indistinguishable at the precision of the data; the truncated-axis bar chart created the impression of a difference by removing the zero and the spread.

  1. Write the reported value for a metric of 0.73819 with a 95 % interval of [0.70, 0.78].

The half-width is about 0.04, one significant figure, two decimals; so the value is reported as 0.74 with the interval [0.70, 0.78]. Reporting 0.73819 claims five significant figures for a quantity known to two. Had the half-width been 0.012, two significant figures would be kept and the value reported as 0.738 — the rule implemented in round_to_uncertainty().

  1. Which number belongs in the abstract: the random-split RMSE or the scaffold-split RMSE?

Both, with the claim attached to the scaffold one. Quoting only the random-split value answers a question nobody asked (how well the model interpolates among chemotypes it has already seen) and is the single most common over-claim in ligand-based modelling papers. The pair also tells the reader how much of the apparent performance was scaffold memorisation — about a sixth of the headline RMSE here.

  1. Your model predicts a compound’s potency. Do you fill in TRIPOD+AI?

No, or only the items that generalise. TRIPOD+AI is written for prediction models whose outcome is a clinical event in people, and most of its items — participants, eligibility, subgroup fairness, calibration in clinical terms — have no referent in a QSAR study. The applicable checklist is the OECD set with a QMRF; TRIPOD+AI becomes the right one the moment the group’s biomedical projects predict a patient outcome. Filling in every checklist for every paper produces long tables of “not applicable” and hides the items that matter.

  1. What must a data-availability statement contain to be useful?

The identity of the source (database, release, accession or query), the location of the derived data (repository with a persistent identifier), the licence, and the checksum or row count that lets a reader confirm they have the same file. “Available from the authors on reasonable request” fails all four and is empirically equivalent to unavailable.

  1. The data came from ChEMBL. What licence can your curated table carry?

CC BY-SA 3.0, the same as the source, because share-alike propagates to derivative works. The code that produced the table can still be MIT: the licence of the data and the licence of the software are separate. A trained model whose parameters encode the data is treated by the group as a derivative of the data.

  1. Describe the reference-integrity check in three steps and state its two failure modes.

For each DOI in the bibliography: request https://api.crossref.org/works/<doi>; with httr2, read the registered title, compare it with the cited title by string similarity, and flag entries below a threshold. It fails in two directions: false alarms, when the registered title contains markup, a subtitle or non-ASCII characters; and misses, when a reference has no DOI at all, which is the case for books, theses and some conference papers — those still require a human check.

  1. What may a language model legitimately do in the preparation of a paper from this laboratory, and what must be disclosed?

It may improve the English of text the authors wrote, draft boilerplate such as availability statements and documentation comments, explain errors and suggest code that is then tested. It may not generate results, write an argument the authors have not made, or supply citations. Its use is disclosed in a short statement naming what it was used for, the authors verify every reference and every number, and authorship remains with the humans who take responsibility.

  1. Why does the laboratory write the figure captions before the Results section?

Because a caption forces the claim to point at visible evidence. If the caption cannot be written in two or three sentences that a reader who skipped the text would understand, the panel is not finished — and the claims that turn out to point at nothing are deleted while deleting them is still cheap. It also fixes the order of the figures, which fixes the order of the argument.

Glossary

Applicability domain
The region of chemical or feature space in which a model’s predictions are considered reliable, stated explicitly and supported by evidence of degradation outside it.
Bootstrap confidence interval
Interval obtained by resampling the test cases with replacement and taking percentiles of the recomputed metric.
Caption contract
The requirement that a caption let a reader who skipped the text understand the panel, name the statistical objects shown, give the sample size, and assert nothing the panel does not show.
cairo_pdf
The R graphics device that writes PDF with the glyphs embedded; the default pdf() device references fonts by name instead.
Data-availability statement
The sentence naming the source, location, licence and identifier of the data behind a paper.
Deuteranopia
The most common colour-vision deficiency, a reduced ability to distinguish red from green; simulated here by a linear transformation of sRGB values.
Figure ordering
The convention that figures run data, method, main result, control, application, and that panels are read left to right as an argument.
LiveCoMS best practices
Community articles specifying what a molecular-simulation paper must report: force field, water model, thermostat, time step, equilibration, replicas and correlation-aware uncertainty.
MIAME / MINSEQE
Minimum-information standards for microarray and sequencing experiments: raw data, processed data, sample annotation, design, platform and protocols, deposited with an accession.
Okabe-Ito palette
An eight-colour categorical palette that remains distinguishable under the common colour-vision deficiencies.
patchwork
The R package that composes complete ggplot2 objects into multi-panel figures with the operators | and / and adds panel letters with plot_annotation(tag_levels).
Perceptually uniform colour map
A sequential map (viridis, cividis, magma) whose luminance increases monotonically, so equal steps in value look like equal steps in colour and the map survives greyscale printing.
QMRF
QSAR Model Reporting Format: the structured document whose nine sections record a model against the five OECD validation principles.
Significant figures tied to uncertainty
The convention of rounding the uncertainty to one significant figure (two if it begins with 1) and the value to the same decimal place.
Theme (ggplot2)
The function holding every non-data appearance setting of a plot; installed globally with theme_set() and shipped with the manuscript as an R file.
TRIPOD+AI
The 2024 reporting guideline for prediction models of clinical outcomes developed with regression or machine learning.
Vector vs raster
Formats that store drawing instructions (PDF, SVG, EPS) versus pixels (PNG, TIFF); vector is resolution-independent and preferred for plots with a moderate number of marks. 
produced <- sort(basename(list.files(WORK)))
cat("files produced by this document:", paste(produced, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## files produced by this document: fig_col.svg, fig_col_150.png, fig_col_300.png, fig_col_base.pdf, fig_col_cairo.pdf, figure1.pdf, figure2_fourpanel.pdf, lbqc_theme.R, supplementary_table_S1.csv, supplementary_table_S1_dictionary.csv
unlink(WORK, recursive = TRUE)
cat("scratch folder removed:", !dir.exists(WORK), "\n")
## scratch folder removed: TRUE

Nothing a document writes outside its own outputs should survive it: the figures, the style file, the supplement and its dictionary were written into the session’s tempdir() and are deleted above. In a real manuscript repository the same objects are written into a tracked figures/ and tables/ folder instead, and the path appears once, at the top of the document.

Textbooks

  • Tufte ER. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. 2nd ed. Graphics Press; 2001. - The source of the data-ink argument and of the vocabulary for discussing chartjunk.
  • Healy K. Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction. Princeton University Press; 2018 (free online). - Why a plot works, with the perceptual evidence, and every example in ggplot2.
  • Wickham H, Çetinkaya-Rundel M, Grolemund G. R for Data Science. 2nd ed. O’Reilly; 2023 (free online). - Chapters on communication and on graphics for export.
  • Schimel J. Writing Science. Oxford University Press; 2012. - The narrative structure of a scientific argument, at paragraph resolution.

Online resources

  • OECD. Guidance Document on the Validation of (Quantitative) Structure-Activity Relationship [(Q)SAR] Models, ENV/JM/MONO(2007)2, and the JRC QMRF template: oecd.org.
  • ICMJE. Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals, section on artificial-intelligence-assisted technology: icmje.org/recommendations.
  • EQUATOR Network, the index of reporting guidelines including TRIPOD+AI, STARD and CONSORT: equator-network.org.
  • patchwork reference and the guide to composing and tagging panels: patchwork.data-imaginist.com.
  • Crossref REST API documentation, used by the reference-integrity check: api.crossref.org.
  • The Turing Way, chapters on research communication and open-access publishing: the-turing-way.netlify.app.
Study material for Data Science for Computational Drug Discovery and Biomedical Research — R edition — Laboratorio de Bioinformática y Química Computacional (LBQC), Universidad Católica del Maule. Knitted from the R-Markdown source U23.Rmd; every figure and number was produced by the R code shown, and the notebook runs in Google Colab (R runtime). The Python edition of this unit is here. Last built 18 October 2026.
